items._ogDesc: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is calling on Ottawa to get back to the negotiating table with the United States before its counter-tariffs take effect in two weeks.
items.body:
EDMONTON — Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is calling on Ottawa to get back to the negotiating table with the United States before its counter-tariffs take effect in two weeks.

Smith, in a statement posted online Tuesday, said tariffs and counter-tariffs only risk further escalating the trade war between Canada and its southern neighbour.

The federal government announced Tuesday its plan to implement retaliatory tariffs starting Sept. 8 on a range of U.S. exports, ranging from steel and aluminum to consumer items, including smartphones and golf clubs.

It also announced relief and support measures for businesses to withstand the trade fight.

Smith said in her statement that she appreciates Ottawa’s plan to support businesses and that her government is working to see if provincial relief is also necessary.

“Alberta’s government remains concerned that tariffs and counter-tariffs increase costs, disrupt supply chains, put pressure on businesses and workers, and ultimately risk escalation to even higher and broader tariffs that will impact even more Canadians,” she said.

“There is still time before these counter-tariffs take effect on Sept. 8, and I am urging the federal government to use that time to get back to the negotiating table with the United States.”

Smith has been a holdout among provincial and territorial leaders when it comes to putting their support behind Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan for counter-tariffs.

The U.S. tariffs kicked in over the weekend, after Careny called off talks while citing unacceptable terms being sought by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.

The premier said Tuesday that her focus is on protecting jobs and businesses in Alberta.

The province wasn’t immediately able to respond to questions about what impact Ottawa’s retaliatory tariffs could have on Alberta’s economy.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said earlier Tuesday that the counter-tariffs will cover 11.3 per cent of his province’s annual imports from south of the border, totalling $1.5 billion worth of goods.

Moe said Tuesday that Ottawa was making the right decision, despite the impact it’s expected to have on Saskatchewan.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 25, 2026.

Jack Farrell, The Canadian Press

items.body:
The federal government has announced its plan to hit the United States with dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs affecting hundreds of American products.

It comes after U.S. President Donald Trump’s 50 per cent tariffs on roughly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect over the weekend after trade talks between the U.S. and Canada broke down.

  • Canada’s new tariffs: A list of key U.S. goods facing surtaxes
  • Trade War Coverage on CTVNews.ca
  • Know first. Know fast. Download the CTV News App.

Trump has made a number of posts to Truth Social Tuesday, expressing his love for French Canadians while openly considering renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

  • Carney says terms presented by the U.S. were a ‘bad deal.’
  • Trump fires back, threatens to increase auto tariffs to 50 per cent.
  • Ford calls Trump a ‘loser,’ ‘king of bankruptcies’
  • Vance accuses Canada of ‘unreasonable last-minute demands’

Follow along for the latest:

Which U.S. imports will be tariffed?

On Tuesday, government officials told reporters that the list of tariffed items were designed to match the U.S. levies on Canadian products, with “individual product rates based on matching the U.S. rate for the same goods.”

For example, tariffs on steel and aluminum imports from the U.S. will now go from 25 to 50 per cent, as will tariffs on furniture and clothing.

Other notable items being tariffed at 50 per cent include:

  • Perfumes and makeup
  • Smartphones
  • Milk products
  • Tableware and kitchenware
  • Plywood products
  • Paper products
  • Honey, molasses and malt extract
  • Doors, windows and frames
  • Cutlery

The list of products being hit with 25 per cent tariffs include:

  • A variety of seafood products
  • Large kitchen appliances
  • Cheese and curd products
  • Carpets and textiles

Spencer Van Dyk Ottawa News Bureau, writer & producer and Stephanie Ha Ottawa News Bureau, manager

Read the full article here

White House alleges pattern of Canadian abuses

The White House released a statement Tuesday afternoon that outlined what it described as a record of Canadian trade abuses against the United States.

The statement, titled “President Trump Is Finally Ending Canada’s Free Ride,” reiterated Trump’s earlier claims that “Canada has been ripping off the United States for decades,” and went on to read that Trump is “done” letting Canada “get away with it.”

According to the release, the U.S. offered Canada the most preferential market access of any country on Earth last week, including deep cuts on steel, aluminum, autos, lumber, and more.

“Instead of partnership, Canada chose unreasonable demands, walk-backs, and flat-out rejection,” the statement read.

The release went on to list what the White House called a “record of Canadian abuse,” including restrictions on American wine, beer and spirits, Canada’s decision to retaliate with tariffs rather than continue negotiations, and its treatment of U.S. aerospace manufacturer Gulfstream, among other complaints.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Consider CUSMA dead’ if counter-tariffs applied: expert

The Canada-U.S. trade dispute could have major consequences for the future of the continental trade agreement, according to one policy expert.

“If those counter tariffs actually go into effect on Sept. 8, you can consider CUSMA dead,” Hannah Thibedeau, executive Communications Officer at Global Public Affairs, said on CTV News Channel Tuesday.

She said the two-week delay before Canada’s retaliatory tariffs take effect provides an important window to de-escalate tensions and potentially revive negotiations.

“The good thing is … there is that off-ramp time frame,” she said, adding that the focus should be on how tariffs could affect Canadians’ finances rather than provocative rhetoric.

Thibedeau said the key question now is whether negotiators can find a way to reach an agreement before the deadline.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

Moe backs ‘targeted’ counter-tariff announcement

Saskatchewan’s premier is voicing support for the federal government’s counter-tariff measures.

In a statement to CTV News Tuesday, Premier Scott Moe said he endorsed the “focused and targeted” response to the 50 per cent tariffs imposed on Canadian goods by the U.S. — affecting roughly $28 billion worth of goods.

According to Moe, the new counter-tariffs will cover about $1.5 billion, or 11.3 per cent, of Saskatchewan’s annual imports from the U.S.

“We are analyzing the counter-tariff list closely and working with affected industries to determine its potential impact on jobs and consumer prices, while also reviewing the federal government’s support measures to ensure they work for Saskatchewan businesses and workers,” the statement read.

Daniel Reech, CTVNewsRegina.ca digital journalist. Read the full article here.

Ford reveals he told PM not to take deal

In an interview with ABC’s Kyra Phillips on Tuesday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford revealed that he told Prime Minister Carney not to take the U.S.’ deal before trade negotiations fell apart last weekend.

“No deal is better than a bad deal,” Ford said, suggesting that Washington’s proposed terms would have “bled out” Canada’s steel and auto industry.

Ford struck a more diplomatic tone Tuesday after a war of words with President Trump a day earlier. The premier admitted to Phillips that the exchange got a “little heated,” after he told Trump to “kiss my ass” over the latest trade salvo.

“I don’t want to make it personal. What I want to do is sign a deal and make sure both countries thrive,” he said.

Phil Tsekouras, CTVNews.ca journalist

White House posts ‘Lake America’ LEGO image

In a post to social media Tuesday, the official White House page posted an AI image of a LEGO-style map of the United States featuring Lake Ontario renamed “Lake America.”

Amid renewed tensions and a worsening trade war between the United States and Canada, U.S. President Donald Trump floated the idea of changing the name of the lake Tuesday morning, saying in a social media post that the U.S. doesn’t “expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

The AI LEGO map does not include Canada, but rather appears to depict it as another body of water.

Also featured on the image is the Gulf of America, which was formerly called the Gulf of Mexico, until Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 to have U.S. departments change it. That decision was controversial at the time and received significant pushback.

Spencer Van Dyk Ottawa News Bureau, writer & producer

Toronto mayoral candidate vows to rename New York, if elected

If Trump is going to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America to spite the province, Toronto mayoral candidate Brad Bradford says two can play that game.

Bradford pointed to New York, which borders the Great Lake with Toronto, and referenced the state’s history in a video shared on social media.

“From 1664 until 1776, it was actually called the Province of New York. It was a British colony and it was named after a duke,” Bradford said in the video, while sitting on a bench facing Lake Ontario. The colony was named in honour of James II of England, the Duke of York.

Should Bradford be elected in the upcoming municipal elections, on Oct. 26 of this year, he says he will revert the state’s name to honour its colonial roots.

“I’m even happy to send him a plaque,” Bradford said. “When President Trump retires, and he can’t retire soon enough, he’ll be able to look out his window, way up in Trump Tower and see the great Province of New York.”

Jokes aside, Bradford says threatening to change the name of a shared body of water between two countries will not dampen Torontonians’ patriotism, who instead can fight back against the new round of tariffs by buying Canadian.

“We can’t change what Washington does, but we can change how Toronto shows up for its own,” he said.

Alex Arsenych, CTVNewsToronto.ca journalist

Feds must negotiate before counter-tariffs start: Smith

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is calling on Ottawa to get back to the negotiating table with the United States before its counter-tariffs take effect in two weeks.

Smith says in a statement posted online that tariffs and counter-tariffs only risk further escalating the trade war between Canada and its southern neighbour.

Smith says she appreciates Ottawa’s plan to support businesses and that her government is working to see if provincial relief is also necessary.

Smith has been a holdout among provincial and territorial leaders when it comes to supporting Carney’s plan for counter-tariffs, after trade talks with the U.S. broke down Friday.

The Canadian Press, Read the full story here

Ottawa’s EI extension a good start: CLC

The federal government’s extension of employment insurance for workers affected by U.S. tariffs was applauded by a group representing Canada’s unions on Tuesday.

“Canada was right to walk away from a bad deal. We continue to stand with the government in refusing to sacrifice Canadian jobs and industries just to get Donald Trump to sign a deal he could tear up tomorrow,” said Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress (CLC).

While Bruske welcomes the measures, she says support for workers “needs to keep pace.”

“Too many workers still fall through the cracks of EI, and for many who qualify, the benefits aren’t enough when a good-paying job disappears,” said Bruske. “The government needs to be ready to go further, making EI easier to access, increase the amount workers receive, and ensuring workers have the support they need for as long as this trade war lasts.”

Hunter Crowther, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘United Team Canada’

A statement from Carney, sent from the Prime Minister’s Office on Tuesday, says he spoke with opposition leaders about the federal government’s response to the “unjustified U.S. tariffs, including the new measures to support Canadian workers, families, and businesses.”

“The Prime Minister and the leaders discussed the ongoing response and underscored the importance of a united Team Canada approach as Canada works to protect jobs, build the economy, and stand up for Canadian interests,” the statement said.

Michael Lee, CTVNews.ca lead morning producer

Poilievre, Carney discuss trade dispute

After announcing plans to meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney on Tuesday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said the two spoke by phone about the escalating trade dispute.

In a social media post, Poilievre outlined several requests he said he made to Carney, including releasing the text of the rejected trade agreement, recalling Parliament and adopting an emergency economic action plan aimed at protecting jobs and lowering costs for Canadians.

“The plan should scrap gas taxes until Canada Day, have zero capital gains tax on reinvesting in Canada, end the industrial carbon tax, green -light the 500 projects waiting for federal permits, and have ZERO sales tax on Canadian-made cars” the post read.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Canada-U.S. now ‘a zero-sum’ relationship

Canada needs to stand up to U.S. President Donald Trump, historian Philip O’Brien says.

“The only way to deal with Trump and not to be constantly badgered and constantly bullied is to stand up to him and say ‘No,’” O’Brien, chair of strategic studies at the University of St Andrews, told CTV News.

O’Brien said Trump is now operating from a weaker position and warned his approach could hurt Republicans in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections.

He said Canadians must also recognize that the U.S. Republican Party has changed and that Trump has reframed the relationship as “a zero-sum,” rather than the mutually beneficial partnership it has historically been.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Good faith’ negotiations needed from U.S.: A.I. Minister

Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon says dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs set to go into effect on Sept. 8 are aimed at protecting workers, the country and Canada’s sovereignty.

Solomon, who was at today’s announcement on retaliatory measures, tells CTV News Channel the United States’ latest trade offer “was not a deal that was going to benefit Canada.”

“That’s why the prime minister and the team walked away,” he says. “But we’re ready to go back when there’s good faith negotiations.”

Pointing to Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s colourful jabs at Trump, Solomon notes “people are angry and people are proud of this country.”

“So I’m not surprised by the language, but we’ve got to be smart and strategic, and that’s what we’re doing with this—September 8th, dollar-for-dollar tariffs,” he says.

Asked whether Canada will have to wait for a new U.S. president to take office before repairing the relationship with the U.S., Solomon was firm in his stance: “We’re not waiting.”

“Let’s be clear, this is not a wait. We are moving ahead. We are going to build. This is business as usual here,” he says.

“We’ve got to control what we can control, and that’s not sitting around waiting and twiddling our thumbs.”

Samantha Pope, senior producer, CTV’s Power Play with Vassy Kapelos

Canada must not show ‘pain points’

Canada’s decision to delay levelling retaliatory tariffs against U.S. goods will give businesses time to adjust their supply chains and avoid shifting the burden onto Canadian consumers, says international trade lawyer Robert Glasgow.

“By giving that trackway, you’re actually giving businesses time to reasonably recalibrate their supply chain,” Glasgow, of KPMG Law, said in an interview with CTV News Channel.

He said companies may have goods already in transit or orders that are too late to cancel, meaning immediate tariffs by Canada could hurt our buyers more than U.S. suppliers.

Glasgow also cautioned against calls to make trade negotiations public, saying doing so could reveal Canada’s “pain points” and give U.S. negotiators a “road map” for where to apply pressure.

Archie Niari, CTVNews.ca journalist

Fate of Honda plant?

A senior Honda executive said the Japanese automaker might not build an eighth assembly plant in North America unless a key trade deal is extended.

Honda executive vice-president Noriya Kaihara told reporters at a roundtable in Washington the automaker is close to full production capacity in North America and needs a new factory.

However, “if there is no USMCA agreement in the future, we may have to change our direction,” Kaihara said, adding the company will need to make a decision within a year or two and would like the plant to be running by around 2030.

Honda indefinitely suspended its Canada EV project, an US$11-billion investment plan to produce EVs and batteries. It also cancelled three planned EVs for the U.S. market.

Last year, Honda said it was shifting production of its U.S.-bound five-door Civic hybrid model from Japan to Indiana.

Read the full article here.

‘The stakes are high’: Global trade expert

Jeff Mahon, the former deputy director at Global Affairs Canada’s China Division, said while retaliatory tariffs have been unleashed, there’s still about $300-billion worth of goods on each side of the border which could still be taxed.

“What that means is, things could spiral out of control. President Trump, as we’ve all seen, can be a loose cannon, so it is quite risky. But at the same time, you do need to stand up to him,” the director of international business and geopolitical advisory at StrategyCorp Inc. told CP24 on Tuesday.

In the interim, Mahon said he’s hoping that “cooler heads prevail” as the two countries look to carve out a new deal, but that getting the U.S. back to the negotiating table will be “very difficult.”

“But this relationship’s too important. This isn’t a ‘one and done.’ Things are going to continue unfolding. Hopefully, we can get to a better situation soon without too much damage,” he said.

“The stakes are high, but let’s not get too carried away.”

Phil Tsekouras, CTVNews.ca journalist

‘Idiotic tariffs and wars’

U.S. Sen. Tim Kaine, a Democrat from Virginia, responded to Trump’s post about renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” saying on social media that “with American troops being killed and injured overseas, and our families and businesses paying more for everything because of idiotic tariffs and wars, this is what Dear Leader is fixated on!”

Kaine served as Hillary Clinton’s vice-presidential running mate during her run for U.S. president in 2016 against Donald Trump.

Michael Lee, CTVNews.ca lead morning producer, with files from The Canadian Press

Trump shares ‘Lake America’ map

After announcing his idea to rename one of the Great Lakes, Trump posted an image to Truth Social of the words “Lake Ontario” crossed out and replaced with an American flag and “Lake America” in gold letters.

Michael Lee, CTVNews.ca lead morning producer

‘Most difficult and unreasonable’

In his third Truth Social post Tuesday targeting Canadians, Trump accused Canada of “‘Ripping Off’ the U.S.A. for decades.”

“They have been charging our Farmers 400% Tariffs, and more. They have driven many wonderful U.S. companies out of business. For 10 years they wouldn’t certify Gulfstream Jets, until I got involved. They wanted 100% of the market for Gulfstream’s Canadian competitor,” he said.

“I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable. They feel entitled, but they are not a State, and will be entitled no longer!”

Twenty minutes later, Trump made another post on Truth Social, saying, “Over the last 10 years, the United States lost, on average, 60 Billion Dollars a year with Canada. No more!”

Michael Lee, CTVNews.ca lead morning producer

‘It got a little personal’: Ford

After a series of heated exchanges between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Monday, Ford told CNN Tuesday that the temperature needs to come down.

“It got a little personal yesterday,” he told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer.

In his interview on the U.S. network, Ford returned to some familiar talking points, emphasizing the importance of a strong partnership between the two countries.

“It’s time to get back to the table and let’s negotiate a fair deal because it is hurting the U.S., it is hurting Canada,” he said.

He called Trump’s threats to stop doing business with Ontario “a lot of rhetoric,” noting that the province is America’s third largest trading partner globally.

Codi Wilson, CP24.com journalist

Minister Champagne on Ford’s brash rhetoric

Federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne was asked during a press conference on Tuesday whether anyone in the federal government asked Ford to tone down his rhetoric.

However, he told reporters that he has learned “not to comment on every remark that is being made on either side of the border.”

“My job, our job here this morning is to fight for Canada, is to fight for workers, is to fight for industries, is to bring the support to make sure we give them a bridge when we have more stability in our economy and certainty in specific sectors affected by the U.S. tariffs,” he said.

“That is what Canadians are expecting from us.”

Chris Fox, CP24.com and CTVNewsToronto.ca managing digital producer Read the full story here

‘Canadian counter-tariffs tend to hit harder’: expert

Canadian businesses are gearing up for a tariff storm, with hurt coming from both sides of the border according to one expert.

Ryan Mallough, speaking for the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB), told CTV News Channel on Tuesday that Canadian counter-tariffs could hurt businesses more than Trump’s.

“That’s going to impact more of our members, we saw that back in 2025, the Canadian counter-tariffs tend to hit harder and those businesses are going to need support as well.”

Trump’s tariffs will impact about 40 per cent of CFIB’s exporters, Mallough said, adding that a third of those affected expect revenue losses of 50 per cent or more.

It will be hard for Canadian exporters to find new markets to sell to, given Europe and Asia’s geographical distance and Canada’s interprovincial trade barriers, Mallough added.

“The geographical limitations and the cost of transport do weigh quite heavily,” he said.

Joe Van Wonderen, CTVNews.ca journalist

N.B. won’t stop supplying electricity: premier

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt says Canada’s trade war with the U.S. has not reached a point where her province would stop supplying electricity to Maine.

Holt said it would be an extremely serious measure to turn off the power to communities who have been friends and neighbours to New Brunswick for generations.

That’s as her Ontario counterpart Doug Ford warned he could cut off his province’s power exports to the U.S. entirely in an interview with The Associated Press.

The Canadian Press. Read the full story here.

MacNaughton warns against ‘rhetorical battle’

A former Canadian ambassador to the United States is warning engaging in “rhetorical battle” with President Trump is not something that’s worthwhile, and is urging politicians to instead focus on reaching out to Americans.

In his own experience communicating with Americans, David MacNaughton notes many of them don’t understand the “depth and the breadth” of their relationship with Canada, whether it be economic or defence.

“I think we should be getting out there, whether it be by social media or actually talking on American television and explaining the facts,” he said to host Marcia MacMillan on CTV News Channel.

“We’ve got to do a better job of informing them and getting them to put pressure on the president of the United States, not thinking that somehow engaging in verbal warfare is going to make a difference. I mean, there’s that old saying about engaging in a contest with a skunk. I won’t get into the details, but you know what I mean.”

For example, Ontario Premier Doug Ford saying he’ll be reaching out to governors and U.S. businesses is the “right answer,” MacNaughton adds.

“We’ve just got to tone down the rhetoric and reach out to reasonable Americans who actually benefit substantially from trade with Canada and because of our defence and security relationship, too,” he says. “A lot of them believe exactly what DJT says. And sometimes he gets close to the facts, but not very often.”

Samantha Pope, senior producer, CTV’s Power Play with Vassy Kapelos

‘I love French Canadians!’

U.S. President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post Tuesday morning that he would “never interfere with Canadians speaking French! In fact, I have never even thought of doing such a stupid thing.”

“This lie was made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support, which he has totally lost, from the people of Quebec. I love French Canadians!” he added.

French was listed as one of the key issues that forced Canada to suspend trade talks.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, has downplayed the language-centred trade issues as a “funny fake story,” but said the sticking points came down to Canada’s push to get big streamers like Netflix to pay a portion of their profits to Canadian or Quebecois content producers.

Michael Lee, CTVNews.ca lead morning producer

‘Lake America’

In a Truth Social post Tuesday morning, Trump said: “The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

It comes less than 24 hours after Trump said he plans to increase tariffs to 50 per cent on all Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts, and steel on New Year’s Day.

Confronted with the news during a radio interview on Monday morning, Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded, “He can kiss my ass as far as I’m concerned.”

The U.S. president previously renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, a change that is now reflected on Google Maps.

Codi Wilson, CP24.com journalist

Read the full article here.

Would never tolerate ‘Lake America’: Ont. mayor

Mississauga, Ont. Mayor Carolyn Parrish says President Trump’s threats to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America” are a “bit of a pipe dream.”

“We’re not going to take that sitting down. We’re going to fight back,” she tells host Todd van der Heyden on CTV News Channel. “I don’t think it’s ever going to happen. We would never tolerate that. We’re more concerned about the trade difficulties we’re having right now than we are with name-calling and changing the name of lakes.”

On trade impacts, Parrish notes small- and medium-sized businesses make up 97 per cent of Mississauga’s employers and 18 per cent of jobs are directly tied to exports to the United States.

“They’re very nervous, and we’re very concerned about them,” Parrish says, adding that work is being done to put together a strategy to assist those businesses. For example, the city is seriously looking into using some of its emergency funds to reduce property taxes for some of those businesses, according to Parrish.

Samantha Pope, senior producer, CTV’s Power Play with Vassy Kapelos

Poilievre says he’ll speak with Carney

At a Tuesday morning news conference in Windsor, Ont., Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he will urge Prime Minister Mark Carney to put Canada first and release details of the proposed trade deal when the two speak later that day.

“Let’s be clear: there are no national secrets in that text. It’s already been shown to the United States administration. The president has seen it. His negotiators have seen it. The United States has seen it. Canadians deserve to see it,” he said.

Kayla Thompson, CTVNews.ca journalist

Retaliatory tariff details

Canada will announce retaliatory tariffs against the U.S. today, multiple sources told CTV News.

Prime Minister Mark Carney previously said dollar-for-dollar retaliatory measures will be in place after Labour Day but has not yet released details.

On Monday evening, the Department of Finance said four ministers including Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will announce the measures Tuesday morning at a local business. Among those present will be Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu.

One source told CTV News in addition to retaliatory tariffs, the federal government will announce an expansion of Employment Insurance (EI) to help domestic workers impacted by U.S. tariffs. The source also said the premiers are expected to be briefed on a call.

With files from CTV News’ Graham Richardson, Stephanie Ha and Abigail Bimman

‘Fall in line’

U.S. President Donald Trump took to Truth Social on Monday with a pointed message to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford: “fall in line” or the consequences from the trade war will be much worse.

The post addresses Carney as “Governor,” an ongoing jab the president has used to target Canadian prime ministers, including Justin Trudeau.

Trump’s message also states that the U.S. is Canada’s “key to survival” and that the days of “ripping off our Farmers, and other Businesses, are OVER!”

Elianna Lev, CTVNews.ca multi-platform writer

U.S. warring with likable ‘in-laws’: analyst

Eric Ham, CTV News’ Washington-based political analyst, says Trump’s brash rhetoric is not being echoed by U.S. governors and lawmakers in states most likely to be impacted by the trade war.

“We heard from the governor of Michigan who said that President Trump igniting this trade war with Canada is like going to war with the in-laws that you actually like,” he told CTV News Channel on Tuesday.

Ham added that Maine’s Republican Sen. Susan Collins is imploring the U.S. to get back to the negotiating table.

Ham said he doesn’t know how the trade war will end, but notes a lot of it will play out in the courts since 25 U.S. states have already brought a lawsuit against Trump regarding tariffs.

Elianna Lev, CTVNews.ca multi-platform writer

Full communities at risk, warns steel union

Thousands more jobs could be at risk as U.S. President Donald Trump continues to escalate trade pressure on Canada, warns the United Steelworkers union.

The Canadian steel industry has already seen roughly 2,000 layoffs since the U.S. imposed a 50 per cent tariff on Canadian steel imports last year, says Meg Gingrich, assistant to the national director at the union, which represents 850,000 members across North America, including 225,000 in Canada.

‘“Our members are often working for industries where the employer is the largest employer in the community. Those are community sustaining jobs,” Gingrich told BNN Bloomberg.

“It’s not just our members’ livelihoods at risk. It’s the full communities.”

The union is calling for stronger buy Canadian procurement policies, supports aimed at keeping workers employed and measures to protect the domestic industry.

Anam Khan, journalist at BNN Bloomberg, Read the full article here

Trade war may rattle states with key U.S. Senate races

Trump’s trade war threatens Republican efforts to address voters’ economic concerns as control of the U.S. Senate hinges on states along the border.

“Imposing new tariffs on Canada is a mistake,” Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, one of Democrats’ top targets this year, said while campaigning Monday.

The issue also puts pressure on Republicans in the border states of Michigan, Ohio and Alaska, and in Iowa, whose main trading partner is Canada.

“Trump is escalating a trade war with Canada for his own vanity,” Michigan’s Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed said on social media, adding that his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, is a “rubber stamp” for such policies.

The Associated Press

American business owners react

Michael Howard II, owner of a furniture business outside Detroit, Mich. said the tariffs will hamper the “ability for us to put food on the table for our family” and affect “the ability for us to give back to our community.”

items.body:
FREDERICTON — A New Brunswick-based cybersecurity firm says it has secured millions of investment dollars to grow its operations in Canada.

Lastwall, founded in Fredericton over a decade ago, builds security software to protect computer networks and cloud services.

An investment equity round led by the Business Development Bank of Canada’s StrongNorth fund raised $16 million for the company.

The New Brunswick Innovation Foundation, an independent non-profit originally created by the New Brunswick government, invested $1.5 million in the company, its largest-ever spend.

Lastwall counts the U.S. Department of Defence and the Canadian government among its clients.

The company’s CEO Karl Holmqvist says the cash provides an opportunity for Lastwall to put its expertise to work locally to showcase to the rest of the world.

Premier Susan Holt says the growth of Lastwall is an example of New Brunswick’s potential as an investment hub for strengthening Canada’s defence capabilities.

Holt says it’s beneficial to have domestic cybersecurity companies so that Canada doesn’t have to rely on foreign businesses.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 25, 2026.

items.title: Target shares drop after Halloween costume backlash
items.description: Target shares slid as much as five per cent after the retailer apologized for and pulled a Halloween costume criticized for evoking Blackface.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A shopper enters a Target store, Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026, in Woodbury, Minn. (AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Ellen Schmidt</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Target shares slid as much as five per cent after the retailer apologized for and pulled a Halloween costume criticized for evoking Blackface.
items.body:
Target shares slid as much as five per cent after the retailer apologized for and pulled a Halloween costume criticized for evoking Blackface, renewing concerns about brand missteps just as its financial turnaround effort had begun to bear fruit.

In an internal email viewed by Reuters, Chief Merchandising Officer Cara Sylvester echoed Target’s public apology on Monday, telling employees the item “never should have been in our assortment” and that the company would “learn from this and do better.”

Still, Wall Street was spooked by echoes of a product misstep around 2023’s Pride Collection and a controversy last year over Target’s decision to roll back its diversity, equity and inclusion policies.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The Halloween costume is “another example ... where Target has lost trust with its consumer base,” said Tejal Patel, executive director of SOC Investment Group, a Target shareholder that has long criticized company leadership.

Morningstar analyst Brett Husslein said the share drop reflected “the fragility of (Target’s) competitive positioning,” noting that it relies on consumer relations and shopping experience to compete with retailers like Walmart and Costco that win on price.

Apology fails to sway

The product, sold as the “Kids’ Glows Under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume,” prompted backlash on social media as some consumers said it resembled a racist caricature evocative of minstrel shows.

“We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners,” Target said in Monday’s statement.

Some stakeholders remained upset.

Sheletta Brundidge, a Minneapolis entrepreneur who last year protested Target’s DEI rollbacks, said the retailer’s apology did not sway her. “Target keeps showing us who they are,” she said.

A post in BlackPeopleofReddit, a Reddit community with 1.6 million members, urged a Target boycott. Several users commented that they had boycotted the company since its DEI reversal.

One commenter wrote, “I don’t see how anyone could look at (the costume) and not notice what it was.”

Other commenters were slower to judgment, with one saying they were “trying to not attribute (the costume) to malice,” and another noting that boycotting Target could backfire by hurting Black-owned brands sold there.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Demonstrating to stakeholders that Target has improved its internal processes might prove more effective than an apology, said Angeli Gianchandani, adjunct instructor at New York University’s School of Professional Studies.

“The fix is a disclosed review process that checks new products and their marketing ... before they reach a shelf,” said Gianchandani, adding that markets tend to tolerate single mistakes, but punish repeated ones.

Fresh controversy revives scrutiny

The backlash steepens the path for a U.S. retailer trying to turn around lagging sales.

New CEO Michael Fiddelke has cut prices and refreshed merchandise, and there are some positive results. The company has reported consecutive strong quarters, with shares up about 70 per cent this year and reaching a near two-year high on Monday.

Target declined to comment on who designed the Halloween costume and did not provide details on the product approval process.

Reporting by Juveria Tabassum in Bengaluru; Editing by Devika Syamnath, Anil D’Silva and Cynthia Osterman

items.title: Doug Ford says its time to turn down the temperature one day after calling Donald Trump ‘a loser’
items.description: Ontario Premier Doug Ford says that it is time to turn down the temperature after “things got a little heated” and a “little personal” with U.S. President Donald Trump one day prior.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Ontario Premier Doug Ford appears on CNN, Tuesday, April 25, 2026.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Ontario Premier Doug Ford says that it is time to turn down the temperature after “things got a little heated” and a “little personal” with U.S. President Donald Trump one day prior.
items.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford made a series of appearances on U.S. television on Tuesday where he conceded that it is time to turn down the temperature after “things got a little heated” and a “little personal” with U.S. President Donald Trump one day prior.

Ford joined CNN, Fox Business and ABC for interviews in which he appeared to tone down his rhetoric, one day after he called Trump a “loser,” a “dictator” and the “king of bankruptcies” during a press conference in Hamilton.

  • Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on 700 U.S. products. Follow for live updates.

The war of words between Trump and Ford erupted after the premier appeared on The Morning Rush with Bill Carroll in Ottawa and said that Trump could “kiss my ass” after the U.S. president vowed to increase tariffs to 50 per cent on all Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts, and steel on New Year’s Day.

Trump, for his part, called Ford the “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford” in a post on Truth Social.

“I think so. Things got a little heated, it got a little personal yesterday between the president and myself but I want to make a deal, a good deal for the American people and a good deal for the Canadians,” Ford said when asked by CNN’s Wolf Blitzer whether it was time to turn down the temperature in his war of words with Trump. “It’s time to get back to the table and let’s negotiate a fair deal because it is hurting the U.S., it is hurting Canada.”

Ford says comments didn’t go too far

Ford’s personal attacks directed at Trump on Monday came after he was asked to respond to Trump’s Truth Social post, in which the U.S. President also referred to Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Ontario premier as “Governor Carney and his flunky, Ford.”

Trump appeared to set his eyes on Ontario again on Tuesday morning, saying in another Truth Social post that the U.S. was “giving serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America since “we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

While Ford did appear to move away from personal criticism of Trump during his televised appearances, he may not be walking back Monday’s rhetoric entirely.

Leaving his office at Queen’s Park on Tuesday, Ford was asked whether he went too far and replied “not at all.”

Ford did not take further questions from reporters.

In his appearance on CNN, Ford said that its “time to get back to the table” and negotiate “a fair deal” to end the trade war with the U.S.

He then called Trump’s threats to stop doing business with Ontario “a lot of rhetoric,” noting that the province is America’s third largest trading partner globally.

“I do not understand why he wants to attack Canada non-stop. We are their closest friends and allies,” he said. “And make no mistake about it: Canadians still love the American people, they love the U.S. They don’t see eye-to-eye with the president by any means but they love the American people and I do as well.”

Ford told reporters on Monday that he has “more brains in my baby toe” than Trump has “in his whole body.”

He then added: “I don’t like the guy. Simple.”

That rhetoric was absent from his U.S. media appearances on Tuesday, however.

In his appearance on Fox Business, Ford also admitted that “things got a little heated” between him and Trump before shifting his focus to the impact that tariffs will have on American workers.

“I feel bad for the autoworkers of Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Kentucky that are going to lose their jobs because we buy 400 per cent more autos (from the U.S.) than any country in the entire world,” he said.

Later in the day, Ford told ABC’s Kyra Phillips that he is not interested in making the dispute between the two countries “personal” and instead wants to “sign a deal and make sure both countries thrive.”

Ford’s appearances on Tuesday came ahead of a news conference where federal officials detailed counter tariffs on 700 different American products.

Federal Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne was asked during that press conference whether anyone in the federal government asked Ford to tone down his rhetoric.

However, he told reporters that he has learned “not to comment on every remark that is being made on either side of the border.”

“My job, our job here this morning is to fight for Canada, is to fight for workers, is to fight for industries, is to bring the support to make sure we give them a bridge when we have more stability in our economy and certainty in specific sectors affected by the U.S. tariffs,” he said. “That is what Canadians are expecting from us.”

items.title: Sask. premier backs ‘targeted’ counter-tariff announcement
items.description: Saskatchewan’s premier is voicing support for the federal government’s counter-tariff measures.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe speaks to reporters on July 21, 2026.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Saskatchewan’s premier is voicing support for the federal government’s counter-tariff measures.
items.body:
Saskatchewan’s premier is voicing support for the federal government’s counter-tariff measures.

In a statement to CTV News Tuesday, Premier Scott Moe said he endorsed the “focused and targeted” response to the 50 per cent tariffs imposed on Canadian goods by the U.S. — affecting roughly $28 billion worth of goods.

On Tuesday, Canada retaliated by announcing dollar-for-dollar tariffs on U.S. imports.

  • Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on 700 U.S. products. Follow for live updates.

Existing tariffs on American goods like steel and aluminium will increase from 25 per cent to 50 per cent.

The retaliatory tariffs will also target U.S. imports such as smartphones, perfumes and makeup, milk products, plywood products, cutlery and doors — all at 50 per cent.

According to Moe, the new counter-tariffs will cover about $1.5 billion, or 11.3 per cent, of Saskatchewan’s annual imports from the U.S.

“We are analyzing the counter-tariff list closely and working with affected industries to determine its potential impact on jobs and consumer prices, while also reviewing the federal government’s support measures to ensure they work for Saskatchewan businesses and workers,” the statement read.

  • Sask. premier says U.S. tariffs are violation of CUSMA deal, supports Canada’s response

However, the premier still expressed concern about the overarching impacts of the trade war.

“While this is the appropriate response to the latest round of US tariffs, we can never lose sight of the fact that all tariffs hurt businesses, jobs, consumers and families on both sides of the border, and our ultimate goal must be to get back to a free and fair trade relationship with the US, as we have enjoyed for many years,” he wrote.

Carney first announced its intention to retaliate and match the tariffs dollar for dollar on Saturday, with the official announcement coming Tuesday.

Moe is scheduled to speak with media about the topic on Wednesday.

items._ogDesc: SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday to build a Starship rocket launch complex in southern Louisiana, a US$100 billion effort poised to transform coastal wetlands into a critical base for the company’s AI satellite launch ambitions.
items.body:
WASHINGTON - SpaceX unveiled plans on Tuesday to build a Starship rocket launch complex in southern Louisiana, a US$100 billion effort poised to transform coastal wetlands into a critical base for the company’s AI satellite launch ambitions.

The 125,000-acre (50,585-hectare) site on Pecan Island, which SpaceX named Starbase, La., will expand the company’s Starship launch operations beyond South Texas and Florida. It will eventually launch thousands of Starship flights a year, SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said.

Construction will begin next year with the first Starship launch in 2029, SpaceX said in a statement. Shotwell detailed the plans near the proposed site in Louisiana’s Vermilion Parish at an event with Gov. Jeff Landry and other senior state officials.

  • Latest updates on company news here

SpaceX plans to build a “self-sustaining” spaceport with its own propellant production, power generation, deep-water shipping capabilities, vehicle processing facilities, and probably an airport, Shotwell said.

The marshland site is more than eight times the size of Manhattan. SpaceX has significantly expanded its U.S. South footprint in recent years, having built a Colossus AI data centre in Tennessee and Mississippi and Starlink facilities in Austin, Texas. It is planning a chip plant in central Texas. Landry called the deal an “inflection point” for Louisiana.

“This project means more than just steel, technology, and capital. It represents jobs for our families. It represents momentum for our communities, and it represents protection for our coast,” he said.

SpaceX said the Louisiana site will add more than 3,000 jobs to the region.

SpaceX has faced backlash, however, from many residents near its sites concerned about water, environmental pollution and pressure to sell land.

SpaceX has for years launched rockets from Cape Canaveral, Fla., Vandenberg Space Force Base in California and Starbase, the company town in South Texas that has been home to its Starship development and test-launch operations.

(Reporting by Joey Roulette; Editing by Mark Porter and Rod Nickel)

Joey Roulette, Reuters

items.title: Trump threatens to change name of Lake Ontario to Lake America
items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump said he is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario amid the ongoing trade dispute between the U.S. and Canada.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[U.S. President Donald Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are shown in this composite image. (Associated Press, Canadian Press)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump said he is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario amid the ongoing trade dispute between the U.S. and Canada.
items.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump said he is considering changing the name of Lake Ontario amid the ongoing trade dispute between the U.S. and Canada.

Trump made the comment in a post on Truth Social on Tuesday morning.

“The United States is giving serious consideration to changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America in that we don’t expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer,” Trump wrote.

“Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

It would not be the first time Trump renamed a body of water. The U.S. president previously renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America, a change that is now reflected on Google Maps.

In a post to social media on Tuesday afternoon, the official White House account shared an image of a Lego map of the United States featuring Lake Ontario renamed ‘Lake America.’

The map did not include Canada, but rather appears to depict it as another body of water.

The U.S. president’s latest threat comes after he and Ontario Premier Doug Ford hurled a string of insults back and forth on Monday.

The bitter exchange began when the U.S. president vowed to increase tariffs to 50 per cent on all Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts, and steel on New Year’s Day.

  • ‘Dumbest trade war in history’: How major media outlets are reacting to the Canada-U.S. tariff fight

Confronted with the news during a radio interview on Monday morning, Ford responded, “He can kiss my ass as far as I’m concerned.”

Trump proceeded to launch a personal attack against Ford, referring to him as “the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford.”

In the same post, Trump called the premier’s comments “lots of bluster” before noting that Canada “couldn’t survive” without the U.S.

He then referred to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ford as “Governor Carney and his flunky, Ford.”

“Someone should get these clowns to “fall in line” or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!” Trump wrote.

Speaking at a news conference in Hamilton later in the day, Ford continued to lash out at Trump, calling him a “loser,” “a bully,” and the “king of bankruptcies.”

“I have been in this game a lot longer than he has. I got skin on me like an alligator and you think an insult from him hurts me? Well bring it on buddy, I am ready. Bring it on,” Ford said.

“We’re going to fight with everything we have and, you know something, I have more courage, more brains in my baby toe than he has in his whole body.”

Talks between Canada and the U.S. on a new trade deal broke down over the weekend, with Carney blaming “last-minute changes in the U.S. proposed terms” that he said were “unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

The U.S. introduced a new round of 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian exports on Saturday, targeting goods worth $28 billion.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Canada announced dollar for dollar retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of items from the U.S., including perfume and cosmetics and smartphones.

Speaking at the news conference, Industry Minister Melanie Joly responded to Trump’s comment on the shared lake, stating that Canadians will “always call it Lake Ontario,” she said.

“While all these shenanigans are happening, we’ll just be smart, we’ll be strategic, and we’ll fight back,” she said.

Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine responded on social media to Trump’s post about Lake Ontario, saying “with American troops being killed and injured overseas, and our families and businesses paying more for everything because of idiotic tariffs and wars, this is what Dear Leader is fixated on!”

Mississauga Mayor Carolyn Parrish says Trump’s Lake Ontario threat is a “bit of a pipe dream.”

“We’re not going to take that sitting down. We’re going to fight back” she told host Todd van der Heyden on CTV News Channel on Tuesday.

“I don’t think it’s ever going to happen. We would never tolerate that. We’re more concerned about the trade difficulties we’re having right now than we are with name-calling and changing the name of lakes.”

‘It got a little personal’

After the series of heated exchanges between Trump and Ford on Monday, Ford told CNN that the temperature needs to come down.

“It got a little personal yesterday,” he told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer on Tuesday.

In his interview on the U.S. network, Ford returned to some familiar talking points, emphasizing the importance of a strong partnership between the two countries.

“It’s time to get back to the table and let’s negotiate a fair deal because it is hurting the U.S., it is hurting Canada,” he said.

He called Trump’s threats to stop doing business with Ontario “a lot of rhetoric,” noting that the province is America’s third largest trading partner globally.

“What’s happening now is we are seeing a decrease in Canadians buying American vehicles,” he said.

“That is going to hurt the American people.”

He described Trump’s attack on Canada as “unprovoked.”

“I do not understand why he wants to attack Canada non-stop,” Ford said.

He added that he “can’t roll over” while the U.S. president threatens Canada’s “sovereignty” and its businesses.

“We are stronger working together rather than attacking each other,” he said.

He did not rule out taking additional retaliatory measures, such as cutting off electricity the province supplies to some U.S. states but said he would “rather send more electricity” if a fair deal can be negotiated.

Ford has previously called for a tough response to tariffs, urging Ottawa to consider measures similar to the ones that were announced by federal ministers on Tuesday.

At Monday’s news conference, Ford said Carney has his full support in walking away from a “bad deal” that would have “hurt Canadian workers and undermined Canadian sovereignty.”

With files from CP24’s Chris Fox, The Canadian Press, and CTV News

items.body:
A senior Honda executive said the Japanese automaker might not build an eighth assembly plant in North America unless a key trade deal is extended.

The Trump administration is currently negotiating with Canada and Mexico over the fate of the free trade deal known as USMCA.

Honda Executive Vice President Noriya Kaihara told reporters at a roundtable in Washington the automaker is close to full production capacity in North America and needs a new factory.

However, “if there is no USMCA agreement in the future, we may have to change our direction,” Kaihara said, adding the company will need to make a decision within a year or two and would like the plant to be running by around 2030.

He said currently Honda is not passing on the costs of tariffs to buyers in North America. The U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on US$20 billion of Canadian products on Saturday, and Canada said it was retaliating effective September 8.

Last year, Hyundai Motor told the administration that uncertainty about USMCA was delaying its investment decisions.

“Early confirmation of USMCA’s extension would immediately unlock over US$20 billion in new American investments,” the automaker said in November. “Every month of ambiguity slows job creation, site selection and technology development.”

With interest in Honda’s hybrid and other fuel-efficient models soaring as oil prices have remained high since the start of the U.S. war with Iran, the automaker had its best July in seven years, with car sales up 36 per cent.

Honda in May scrapped its long-term EV sales target, including its goal of having EVs make up a fifth of its new car sales in 2030. It now plans 15 new hybrids by 2030.

The Japanese automaker indefinitely suspended its Canada EV project, an US$11 billion investment plan to produce EVs and batteries. It also canceled three planned EVs for the U.S. market.

Last year, Honda said it was shifting production of its U.S.-bound five-door Civic hybrid model from Japan to Indiana.

items.title: Nesto deal leads Canada's near-US$1B fintech investment surge
items.description: Nesto's landmark raise and a Q2 rebound signal a more selective phase for mortgage fintech
items.content: <p>Nesto's landmark raise and a Q2 rebound signal a more selective phase for mortgage fintech</p><img src="https://ca.res.keymedia.com/files/image/iStock-business-meeting-silhouette-serious-tension-638035114.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Nesto's landmark raise and a Q2 rebound signal a more selective phase for mortgage fintech
items.body:
Investment in Canadian fintechs neared US$1 billion in the first half of 2026, as a concentrated burst of second-quarter activity anchored by a landmark mortgage technology deal revealed investors prioritising scale-ready companies over volume.

According to KPMG International's H1'26 Pulse of Fintech report, compiled using PitchBook data, Canadian fintechs attracted US$996.7 million across 47 deals in the period. That's broadly stable against the US$1 billion across 56 deals recorded in the second half of 2025.

On a year-over-year basis, total deal activity fell more than 40% from the US$1.7 billion across 82 deals recorded in H1 2025.

Activity was skewed toward the final quarter of the half. Just US$375 million was deployed across 24 deals in Q1, compared with US$621.7 million across 23 deals in Q2.

The quarter's defining transaction was a US$218.6 million Series E investment in Montréal-based online mortgage lender Nesto, which the round valued at US$1 billion.

New investors included La Caisse (formerly CDPQ), Fidelity Investments Canada, PICTON Investments and Endeavor Catalyst, joining existing backers Portage, Diagram, NAventures, Fonds de solidarité FTQ and Fondaction.

Nesto reported more than $37 billion in mortgage originations in 2026 and manages over $80 billion in mortgages under administration across its three brands — Nesto, CMLS and Nesto Cloud.

Dubie Cunningham, a partner in KPMG Canada's Banking and Capital Markets practice, says the decline in deal count reflects deliberate prioritisation rather than a retreat from Canadian fintech.

"Canadian fintech has entered a selective maturation phase, with investors going after fewer deals but applying more scrutiny to their investments. They are being more discerning and going after fintechs that have scale, specialized AI capabilities and that are competitively positioned to take advantage of upcoming reforms to Canada's financial services industry," Cunningham said.

AI dominates deal activity

AI and machine learning-oriented fintechs attracted 19 investments in H1 2026, more than any other vertical. Digital assets ranked second, highlighted by Robinhood Markets Inc.'s US$168.4 million acquisition of Toronto-based WonderFi Technologies, owner of regulated cryptoasset platforms Bitbuy and Coinsquare.

Venture capital investment reached US$492.9 million across 33 deals in the half, with US$398.2 million deployed in Q2 alone.

Cunningham said capital is flowing to companies using AI to solve specific problems in lending, payments and deposit-taking, not broad digital experimentation.

Brokers navigating the competitive pressures of the open banking era will recognise that technology that accelerates client outcomes is drawing the most attention.

Regulatory reform as the next investment catalyst

Andrew Mathias, a partner in KPMG's Deal Advisory practice, says the Consumer-Driven Banking Act and the Real-Time Rail will reshape competitive dynamics in financial services, opening infrastructure that mortgage technology companies are already positioning to exploit.

"Consumer-Driven Banking and the Real-Time Rail are opening up the infrastructure that fintechs need to compete, and these regulatory reforms could materially alter fintech economics and create conditions for a new period of competition in financial services," Mathias said.

The two reforms are expected to lower the cost of new services, ease income and asset verification for mortgage applications, and reduce fintech dependence on incumbent institutions.

Mathias said the result will be more competition and consolidation across Canadian financial services over the next 12 to 18 months. Nesto's plans to accelerate AI-driven underwriting following its Series E are detailed in a separate Canadian Mortgage Professional analysis.

Globally, KPMG recorded US$103 billion invested across 2,098 fintech deals in H1 2026, with US$81 billion concentrated in the United States.

items.title: Alberta's flat insolvency total hides a bankruptcy shift
items.description: Alberta insolvencies rose, but bankruptcies jumped
items.content: <p>Alberta insolvencies rose, but bankruptcies jumped</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639232796222977257.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Alberta insolvencies rose, but bankruptcies jumped
items.body:
Alberta's consumer insolvency count barely moved in the second quarter of 2026, but the composition of those filings shifted in a direction mortgage brokers should watch closely.

The province recorded 4,932 consumer filings from April to June, up just 1.4% year over year, according to the Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy (OSB).

Canada overall saw filings climb 6.9% to 37,523 over the same period, with Ontario up 10.2% and British Columbia up 10.9%.

On the surface, Alberta appears contained. Underneath, the split between filing types changed meaningfully. Bankruptcies reached 800 in Q2 2026, up 11.3% from a year earlier and 7.8% from the first quarter.

Consumer proposals, the more structured repayment alternative, fell 0.3% to 4,132. 

Read more: Behind Canada's debt slowdown, one province still struggles

What the shift from proposals to bankruptcy signals

A consumer proposal is a legal arrangement allowing a debtor to repay part of what they owe from monthly income over three to five years, while keeping their assets. Bankruptcy discharges debt entirely and is typically the option when no surplus income remains.

Robert Johnson, CPA, CA, CIRP, a Licensed Insolvency Trustee at Moses Advisory Group in Edmonton, described what the data indicates.

"When bankruptcies rise and consumer proposals stay flat, it usually means people are arriving in a deeper financial position where they cannot commit to three to five years of structured repayments in a consumer proposal," Johnson said.

"At that point, bankruptcy is the only filing that clears the debt."

Consumer proposals still accounted for 83.8% of Alberta's consumer filings in Q2 2026, one of the highest proportions of any province. But the direction is moving against that figure. Mortgage brokers working with clients managing heavy non-mortgage debt loads will recognise the pattern, particularly as the two hotspots currently driving Canada's insolvency surge have demonstrated how quickly softening home values can close off refinancing as a debt management tool.

Alberta consumer insolvency filings

Source: Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy, Insolvency Statistics in Canada, Q2 2026. Consumer filings only; business insolvencies excluded. Dash (—) indicates comparative year-over-year data not available.

Edmonton versus Calgary: diverging paths

Alberta's two largest markets moved differently. Edmonton recorded 1,553 consumer filings in Q2 2026, down 3.0% year over year. Calgary recorded 1,413, up 1.7%.

The headline divergence, however, masks a shared compositional trend: Edmonton bankruptcies rose 2.5% while proposals fell 4%, tracking the provincial pattern across both cities.

The backdrop matters for mortgage professionals. Alberta holds the highest 90-plus-day non-mortgage delinquency rate in the country at 2.45%, against a national rate of 1.76%, according to Equifax Canada's Market Pulse Quarterly Consumer Credit Trends and Insights report for Q2 2026.

Alberta business insolvencies climbed to 99 in Q2 2026, up 35.6% year over year — driven partly by tariff-related cost pressures and elevated fuel prices — against a national business filing increase of just 0.2%.

items.title: BC real estate agent fined $200k for exploiting affordable housing program
items.description: A Victoria real estate agent who rented out a unit he was ineligible to buy faces a six-month licence suspension
items.content: <p>A Victoria real estate agent who rented out a unit he was ineligible to buy faces a six-month licence suspension</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639232788655132921.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A Victoria real estate agent who rented out a unit he was ineligible to buy faces a six-month licence suspension
items.body:
A Victoria, British Columbia real estate agent has been fined $200,000 and handed a six-month licence suspension after BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA) found he purchased a subsidised housing unit under false pretences, then immediately rented it out for profit.

Jason Alexander Leslie, a trading services representative who operated through Jason Leslie Personal Real Estate Corporation at RE/MAX Generation in Victoria, entered a consent order with BCFSA on August 14, his second disciplinary action with the regulator.

The order, issued under the Real Estate Services Act (RESA), found Leslie committed both professional misconduct and conduct unbecoming a licensee in connection with his 2018 purchase of a unit in the Vivid at the Yates development in Victoria.

The Vivid building was part of a BC Housing Affordable Home Ownership Program backed by a $52.9 million provincial low-interest loan, with residential units selling at an average of 12% below current market rates.

Eligibility was restricted to households earning no more than $150,000 annually, and purchasers were required to make the unit their primary residence.

Canadian Mortgage Professional first reported on broader exploitation of the Vivid program in 2024, when BC Housing filed 13 lawsuits to recover units from buyers who had not lived in their homes as required.

Leslie signed a statutory declaration on February 13, 2018, claiming to be a qualified purchaser under the Section 219 Affordable Home Ownership Covenant, a document he signed before a notary public.

BCFSA investigators later confirmed he had no intention of residing in the unit at the time of purchase. He also acted as his own buyer's agent in the transaction, collecting a commission of 3% on the first $100,000 and 1.5% on the balance of the adjusted net purchase price.

A British Columbia submortgage broker who continued arranging mortgages for nearly a year after losing her registration has been hit with $55,000 in penalties — the maximum fine available under the province's Mortgage Brokers Act (MBA).https://t.co/V9tWVF4qPR — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) July 15, 2026

Rented out within weeks

Leslie took possession of Unit 102 on May 7, 2021. By June 10, 2021, or less than five weeks later, he had entered a residential tenancy agreement with a third-party tenant. That's a direct violation of the Section 219 Covenant, which prohibited rental to anyone other than qualified persons who were registered owners.

In a written submission to BCFSA, Leslie acknowledged he never intended to make the unit his primary residence.

He also confirmed to investigators that he had acted as buyer's agent for five other clients purchasing units in the same development — three of them in the affordable housing portion — and had explained the program's eligibility requirements to those buyers.

BC Housing conducted an audit in March 2022 and notified Leslie he was ineligible to have purchased the unit.

He returned it to BC Housing in September 2022, repaying the net commission earned on the original purchase, the net rental income collected, the property transfer tax BC Housing incurred, and the legal fees associated with the transaction.

Prior discipline and expanded enforcement powers

This is not Leslie's first BCFSA sanction. A 2019 consent order found he and his corporation committed professional misconduct as a limited dual agent by failing to disclose material facts and allowing an inspection without all sellers' consent. That matter resulted in a $7,500 penalty, $1,500 in costs, and mandatory remedial education.

The latest order includes a further remedial education course at his own expense, as well as 12 months of enhanced brokerage supervision by a managing broker following his suspension.

The case arrives as BCFSA prepares to significantly expand its enforcement powers under British Columbia's new Mortgage Services Act (MSA), which comes into force on October 13, affecting more than 7,000 licensed mortgage professionals in the province.

"The $200,000 penalty and six-month licence suspension sends a clear message: exploiting an affordable homeownership program for personal gain is serious misconduct that erodes public confidence in real estate professionals and will result in significant consequences," said Jon Vandall, senior vice president of financial professionals at BCFSA.

items.title: Downtown Eastside Project Breaks Ground With Funding From Feds, BC Builds, UBC
items.description:
A new mixed-use development is now under construction in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside, thanks in large part to funding and contributions from four different governments in conjunction with those from several other parties.

The project is set for 315 Main Street (also known as 172 East Cordova Street), a corner lot located at the southwest corner of the intersection of Main Street and East Cordova Street.

The site was previously occupied by a low-rise commercial building constructed in 1974, and was sold in July 2024 for $14,500,000 in a transaction brokered by Corbel Commercial.

The project is being led by MAC Development and Housing Society, a partnership between Lu’ma Native Housing Society, Frog Hollow Neighbourhood House, and the Affordable Housing Non-Profit Rental Association.

315 Main Street (172 East Cordova Street) in Vancouver. (Corbel Commercial)

A development application for the site has been in progress since 2021, with a proposal for a multi-coloured 11-storey mixed-use building with 118 social housing units, office space, retail space, theatre space, as well as educational space. The development permit was issued earlier this year, in February.

Earlier this month, construction commenced with a groundbreaking ceremony, where $96 million in funding for the project was also announced.

The Government of Canada is contributing $41.9 million through the Affordable Housing Fund, BC Housing — through BC Builds — is contributing $17.7 million, and the University of British Columbia — which will be relocating its UBC Learning Exchange from its current home at 612 Main Street — is contributing $12.5 million. The Province is also contributing an additional $403,750 through the Mass Timber Demonstration Program.

City of Vancouver records indicate that the City owns the site, and a press release from earlier this month notes that the City is providing $14.5 million in land lease contributions, plus $2.7 million in waivers, to MAC Development and Housing Society, which is contributing $2.4 million. The Metro Vancouver Regional District is providing $1.2 million in waivers, and TransLink is providing $258,900 in waivers.

Ground broke on the project on August 11. (Sunita Dhir - MLA Vancouver-Langara, Facebook)

As the project is proceeding with funding from BC Builds, the 118 units will be provided at affordable rates. In their own press release, the Province said that 79 units will be provided for middle-income households — a focus of BC Builds — with nearly 50% of the units provided at 20% below market rates. The remaining 39 units will be “deeply affordable” and provided to people on income assistance.

The Province says “The target tenant group includes people with a range of low and middle incomes, particularly multigenerational families, seniors, Indigenous Elders, and people with disabilities” and says the function and appearance of the building “aim to celebrate the histories of Indigenous, Chinese-Canadian, Japanese-Canadian and other communities that have long called the Downtown Eastside home and are expected to be reflected among the future residents of the building.”

The Province’s press release also notes that UBC has “bought” the 10,000 sq. ft on the ground floor and second floor. The UBC Learning Exchange offers free educational programs and leadership opportunities, such as English conversation sessions and digital literacy workshops that members can train to lead. The community theatre planned for the ground floor is then “intended to be leased by a non-profit society to provide space for use by local community arts groups.”

“Through consultation with residents and local groups, this new housing has been designed in partnership to meet the unique needs of the community it serves,” said Minister of Housing and Municipal Affairs Christine Boyle. “By taking a heritage-conservation approach that prioritizes continuity and connection, this project honours the neighbourhood’s rich history, celebrates the diverse communities that have shaped the Downtown Eastside and builds on the community-based resources already in place.”

items.title: BMO reveals Q3 financials
items.description: Earnings season is underway as the country’s top banks post their financial results for the third quarter
items.content: <p>Earnings season is underway as the country’s top banks post their financial results for the third quarter</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639232618418144727.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Earnings season is underway as the country’s top banks post their financial results for the third quarter
items.body:
Bank of Montreal (BMO) posted stronger Q3 financials than expected, with adjusted net income of $2.86 billion up 19% from the same time last year even as the headline reported figure slipped.

The company said on Tuesday morning that overall net income was down to $1.75 billion from $2.3 billion, dragged down by a $962 million goodwill charge tied to the announced sale of BMO’s Transportation Finance and Vendor Finance business.

Adjusted earnings per share were 22% higher, climbing to $3.96 from $3.23, while the bank said adjusted return on equity was up to 14% compared with 12% a year before.

Tuesday marked the first day of the Big Six bank’s quarterly earnings announcement, with Scotiabank also revealing its third-quarter results. Toronto-Dominion (TD) Bank, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC), Royal Bank of Canada (RBC), and National Bank of Canada (NBC) are all scheduled to release their earnings in the coming days.

Financial markets will be closely watching provisions for credit losses at Canada’s banking giants as economic uncertainty continues – and BMO set aside less money for souring loans compared with 2025’s third quarter.

Total PCLs fell to $722 million from $797 million a year earlier, the bank said. Year-to-date, BMO’s provision for credit losses has declined to $2.2 billion from $2.86 billion over the same period in 2025.

BMO’s domestic personal and commercial banking division posted adjusted net income of $983 million, a 15% year-over-year jump, driven by a 6% increase in revenue and lower PCLs.

Net interest margin expansion contributed significantly to revenue growth alongside gains in non-interest income.

In the US, BMO’s banking division also saw growth, with adjusted net income rising by 11% to $925 million. Stronger net interest margin and non-interest income fuelled a 5% jump in revenue on the US side, while a stronger US dollar added about two percentage points to that uptick.

The bank announced a fourth-quarter common dividend of $1.71 per share, unchanged from the prior quarter but 5% higher than a year ago. BMO also repurchased 3.8 million common shares at an average price of $239.37 and announced plans to establish a new normal course issuer bid for up to 25 million shares pending regulatory approval.
